speaker: maya
text: Last time: Cahokia, corn, and millions of people who'd never heard of Europe. This time a Genoese sailor gets the math wrong, sails west for Asia, and hits a continent that wasn't lost, then gets its people's name wrong for five centuries. Three boxes: the Columbian Exchange, the encomienda system, the Treaty of Tordesillas. Circle the ones you couldn't explain right now. Eight minutes, and they're yours.

speaker: marcus
text: Start with the why. Europe is hungry for Asian spices and silk, and the old land routes run straight through Ottoman territory. After 1453, when Constantinople falls, those routes get pricier and shakier. Motive one is on the screen: gold.

speaker: maya
text: God is word two up there. What's the church got to do with ships?

speaker: marcus
text: Spain just finished the Reconquista, centuries of war pushing Muslim rule out of Iberia, ending at Granada in 1492. A crown that just won a holy war feels owed new souls. Motive two: God.

speaker: maya
text: And glory is Portugal getting rich off the sea road to Asia while Spain watches from the shore.

speaker: marcus
text: No rival crown watches that quietly. And Spain's not even rich. The Reconquista was expensive. What they've got is a navy, a grudge, and perfect timing. Gold, God, glory. The Spanish business plan.

speaker: maya
text: So how does Portugal crack the ocean first?

speaker: marcus
text: A prince who never sails. Henry the Navigator bankrolls voyage after voyage down the African coast. Look at him: a courtier, not a captain. He buys the voyages; other men risk the water.

speaker: marcus
text: And his captains get four tools that change everything. One: the caravel, small and fast, built to turn on a dime. Two: lateen sails, triangular ones that let a ship claw into the wind. Three: the astrolabe, reading latitude off the stars. Four: the magnetic compass, for holding a course.

speaker: maya
text: Four tools. That's the whole revolution?

speaker: marcus
text: Four tools, and an ocean that used to eat ships.

speaker: marcus
text: Sailors called the open Atlantic the sea of darkness, and you're looking at why. Every mile south was past the edge of every map they owned.

speaker: marcus
text: Then 1488: Bartolomeu Dias rounds the southern tip of Africa. 1498: Vasco da Gama reaches India. Portugal owns the sea road to Asia, and Spain needs another way in.

speaker: maya
text: So Spain finds a Genoese sailor with a wild pitch. Niña, Pinta, Santa María. I know those from a second-grade song, and the tune's still in my head.

speaker: marcus
text: Three little ships, and the smallest idea in naval history.

speaker: marcus
text: Columbus figures Asia sits a few thousand miles west of the Canaries. That's the left side of your screen. The real number is closer to ten thousand. That's the right side. He gets the shape of the earth right and the size of the trip wildly wrong.

speaker: maya
text: So he fails upward into a continent.

speaker: marcus
text: October 12, 1492, the Bahamas. He calls the people he meets Indians because he's sure he's reached Asia, and he dies still insisting it. Four voyages: the Caribbean, the Venezuelan coast, Central America. Never the Asia he was chasing.

speaker: maya
text: Five centuries of calling people by the wrong name. That's got to be a record.

speaker: marcus
text: Now Spain's holding islands, and Portugal is furious. They'd spent decades mapping that African route. So in 1494, Spain and Portugal sign the Treaty of Tordesillas. Box one. See the line on the map: 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde islands, a league's roughly three miles. West of the line goes to Spain. East goes to Portugal.

speaker: maya
text: Let me guess. France and England just agreed to that?

speaker: marcus
text: They ignored it completely.

speaker: marcus
text: But Spain and Portugal mostly honored it, which is why Brazil speaks Portuguese today. Watch the map: the bulge of Brazil sticks out east of the line, onto Portugal's side.

speaker: maya
text: An imaginary line splitting the planet, and it held. Checking box one.

speaker: marcus
text: After 1492, the traffic starts: crops, animals, people, and diseases, moving both directions across the Atlantic. In 1972 the historian Alfred Crosby gave it a name: the Columbian Exchange. Box two.

speaker: maya
text: So that's the trade part. Potatoes one way, sugar the other?

speaker: marcus
text: Bigger than trade, and nobody signed anything. Eastbound: maize, potatoes, tomatoes. They help fuel population growth across Europe.

speaker: marcus
text: Westbound: wheat and sugarcane, plus horses, cattle, and pigs. The Americas had never seen any of them. Picture a prairie with no horses, then picture it with. That's the Exchange in one image.

speaker: maya
text: What about the diseases? Which way did those go?

speaker: marcus
text: Mostly west, and catastrophic. Smallpox, measles, influenza. The faces in this manuscript are living through it. In the hardest-hit places, eight or nine out of ten people die.

speaker: maya
text: And east? Anything go east?

speaker: marcus
text: The one that might have is syphilis, and historians still argue about that one.

speaker: maya
text: Box two, checked.

speaker: marcus
text: So how do a few hundred Spaniards topple empires? Follow the chain: steel weapons and armor, then horses, then above all, disease. But no single link does it alone. It's the combination, plus alliances with Indigenous peoples who had their own reasons to fight the Aztecs. This painting was made by their descendants.

speaker: maya
text: So it wasn't the guns.

speaker: marcus
text: Guns helped, but early guns were slow to reload and miserable in the rain. The real killers were invisible.

speaker: maya
text: And then the encomienda. Box three. What am I looking at?

speaker: marcus
text: Native labor, granted by the crown to a colonist. That's what the mines in this engraving are running on. The deal on paper: the colonist gets the labor of a group of Native people, and owes them protection and Christianization in return.

speaker: maya
text: So it's slavery with paperwork?

speaker: marcus
text: Close enough that historians argue about where the line is. Legally it wasn't chattel slavery. The crown insisted these were free subjects of the king. In practice, the work quotas were brutal and the protection was mostly theoretical. Look at the faces doing the work: that's the reality the paperwork covered.

speaker: maya
text: Checking the last one. Protection in very large air quotes.

speaker: maya
text: Okay. That was a lot of ocean. Three boxes, let's land them. Box one: the Treaty of Tordesillas. 1494, the pope's line, 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde islands. Spain gets the west, Portugal gets the east. Brazil ends up speaking Portuguese.

speaker: marcus
text: Clean.

speaker: maya
text: Box two: the Columbian Exchange. Crosby named it in 1972. Crops and animals and people and disease, moving both ways. Memory check: in the hardest-hit places, eight or nine out of ten died, and the dying went mostly… east? No. West. Disease went west.

speaker: marcus
text: West. Smallpox and measles sailed with the colonists.

speaker: maya
text: Box three: encomienda. The crown grants a colonist Native labor, and the colonist owes protection and conversion back.

speaker: marcus
text: Note the direction. The labor was already there. That's the whole point.

speaker: maya
text: Right. And the protection part deserves the biggest air quotes in history.

speaker: marcus
text: It does.

speaker: maya
text: Two questions, AP-shaped. Say your answer out loud before I do. First, stimulus style: a Spanish priest in the 1550s writes that Native villages "stand empty, the fields untilled, for the sickness took the workers." What's the bigger pattern this source points to?

speaker: maya
text: The Columbian Exchange's disease front. Population collapse on a scale that broke Native communities and fed the demand for coerced labor. Second: in 1494, Spain and Portugal sign an agreement splitting new lands along a line 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde islands. Name it, and explain Brazil.

speaker: maya
text: The Treaty of Tordesillas. Brazil bulges east of the line, so it landed on Portugal's side. That's why it's the one country in South America that speaks Portuguese.

speaker: maya
text: They sailed west looking for Asia — and found a world.

speaker: marcus
text: Next time: England crashes the party. Drake, a vanished colony, and an Armada.

speaker: maya
text: Check your three boxes.
